**On Thresholds**

There's a small piece of psychology research I think about more than I probably should. It's called the doorway effect. Researchers found that when people walk through a doorway, they become measurably worse at remembering what they were just thinking about. Not catastrophically—you don't forget your name—but the thing you got up to do, the object you were carrying in your mind, gets slightly blurred, as if the frame of the door were a squeegee dragged across the glass of attention. The explanation offered is that the brain treats a room as an "event," and crossing into a new room closes the old file and opens a fresh one. Whatever wasn't saved gets partially lost.

I love this finding not because it explains why I've stood in kitchens wondering what I came for—everyone has their own theory about that—but because it suggests that architecture is quietly editing us all day long. Every door is a small forgetting. Every hallway is a corridor of amnesia. We build boxes to live in, and the boxes turn out to be chapter breaks.

Once you notice this, you start seeing thresholds everywhere, and you start noticing how much ceremony we've piled on top of them. The Romans had a god just for doorways, Janus, with two faces looking in opposite directions, and named the first month of the year after him. Brides get carried over thresholds. Mezuzahs are nailed to doorframes. In some households you take your shoes off; in others you knock three times; in a few you are supposed to say something before entering, a formula, a greeting, a spell. Vampires, famously, cannot cross a threshold without invitation—a rule that has always struck me as a beautiful piece of folklore because it treats the doorway as a legal instrument. The house itself has standing. It can refuse you.

We do this because we intuit, without needing a laboratory, that the door changes something. It's not just the wall that separates outside from inside; the door is the place where the separation becomes negotiable, and anything negotiable requires ritual to keep it from being frightening.

I've been thinking about smaller thresholds too, the ones we don't build out of wood. The moment right before you say something you can't take back. The half-second after you've pressed send. The last page of a book you loved, when you're aware that you are about to become a person who has finished it and can never again be a person who hasn't. There's a particular feeling to standing in these places—a kind of delicious dread, a sense that the file is about to close. I suspect we linger there on purpose. We reread the message. We hold the last page. We stand in the doorway with a hand on the frame, not quite leaving.

The word for this, in anthropology, is liminality, from the Latin *limen*, threshold. Victor Turner wrote about liminal states in rites of passage: the initiate is no longer a child but not yet an adult, has been stripped of the old status and not yet given the new one. He noticed that people in this in-between state often develop an intense camaraderie with each other, a leveling of ordinary hierarchy. Nobody is anybody yet, so everybody is equal. It's the same feeling you get in airports at four in the morning, or in hospital waiting rooms, or in the strange week between Christmas and New Year's when nobody quite knows what day it is. The rules are suspended because the room you're in doesn't count. You're in the doorway.

I think the reason these places can feel both unbearable and oddly restful is that they are the only spaces where you are allowed not to be anything in particular. Everywhere else demands a role. The threshold demands nothing; it just asks you to wait. And waiting, for all its bad reputation, is one of the few states in which a person can simply exist without producing.

There's a version of this at the scale of a single day. Morning is a threshold. You are not yet the person who will have the day; the day is still a set of unopened rooms. This is why the first cup of coffee feels sacramental to so many people—not because of the caffeine, or not only, but because it's a small rite conducted at the edge of the ordinary, before you've crossed into it. Evening has its own threshold, the hour when the work is done but sleep hasn't come, when the mind roams around the empty house of the day picking up the things it left in various rooms. People call this hour melancholy, and it can be, but it's also where most of the honest thinking happens. You can only see a room clearly once you've stepped out of it.

I'll admit there's something I find consoling in the doorway effect specifically, in the mechanics of it. It means forgetting isn't always a failure. Sometimes it's structural, a feature of how we're built to move through space. The brain closes the file because it is trying to be ready for the next room. It assumes—optimistically, maybe—that whatever is coming deserves your full attention, more than whatever you just left. Every doorway is a small act of faith that the next room will matter.

Which means, if you want to remember something, you should say it out loud before you cross. Give it a body. Let it walk through the door with you instead of staying behind on the counter. The old rituals knew this: you touch the doorframe, you say the words, you carry the thing across on purpose. The threshold takes what you don't hold onto, and it lets you keep what you carry deliberately.

I don't have a grand conclusion. This is not the kind of thought that arrives at one; it's the kind you carry around like a stone in a pocket, turning it over. But I notice that I've become gentler with myself about standing in doorways—the literal ones, blinking, wondering what I came for, and the other ones too. Some part of me is just closing a file. Some part of me is getting ready for the next room. It's all right to stand there a moment, one hand on the frame, before going in.
